title: Atlas of AI
subtitle: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence
pitch: AI is not weightless or magic. Crawford follows it to the mines, warehouses, datasets and state agencies it depends on, and asks who it serves.

chapters.g: AI as a material and political system, not just clever code.
The minerals, energy and water that computing needs, and the places that pay for it.
The hidden human work behind AI, from warehouse workers to data labelers.
How training data is gathered, often without consent, and treated as a free resource.
How labelling people into categories bakes in old assumptions and harms.
The weak science behind systems that claim to read emotions from faces.
How AI tools grew out of and feed back into military and police power.
AI mostly concentrates power in those who already have it.
Tech billionaires' space dreams as an escape from the planet AI helps to use up.

ideas: AI depends on extraction: of minerals, labour and data.
Classification systems carry politics inside them.
Emotion recognition rests on contested science.
The key question about AI is power: who gains and who pays.

args.a: AI is best understood as an extractive industry that concentrates power.
args.c: Supporters point to real benefits in science, medicine and access to knowledge that this framing can underplay.

args.a: Focusing on present harms matters more than speculative future risks.
args.c: Others argue both matter, and that the same concentration of power makes catastrophic risks more likely, not less.

questions: What physical resources did the last AI tool you used depend on?
Should people be able to refuse having their data used for training?
Can AI be built in a way that spreads power instead of concentrating it?
